catalog_citation: de Voogt, Alex. 2009. A sketch of Afitti phonology. Studies in African Linguistics 38(1): 35-52.
catalog_locator: Section 8 'Tone and Stress', pp. 46-48 (also Section 5 vowels, p. 44, on lengthening under stress)
catalog_quote: Afitti is a tone language with stress. Tonal minimal pairs are attested for monosyllabic, bisyllabic and trisyllabic words, but in longer words stress seems to play a more important role. ... Informants corrected longer words for stress rather than for tonal patterns, accepting different tonal patterns but insisting that stress remain fixed. The stressed syllable is marked by a combination of duration, volume and change in tone, rather than just tone alone. ... Afitti has only two phonemic tones with strong and clear downdrift, with no third tone or even downstep. ... In “short” words, those consisting of fewer than five syllables, stress can be placed on different syllables as long as the tonal pattern remains in place. Since stress commonly coincides with a change in tone it is not clear whether the tonal system is complicated by stress in long words or a tone system is being reduced …

new_statements.quote: All examples are from NYIMANG, unless otherwise stated. ... 2. Tone and Stress 2a. There appear to be three tone levels; dynamic tone occurs only when disyllables are reduced: kégél or kél earth[.] Lexical tone doublets have been recorded ... Tone also has grammatical function (see §§ 4a (iii) and 9a). Stevenson's examples are only tone-marked when tone is of lexical or grammatical significance. 2b. Stress also appears to distinguish words: 'iburan body bt'ran adulteress ibarondl large turtle baro'nd1 poor [scanned of stress-marked Nyimang forms] Stress is not marked in other examples given here, however. 3. Word Shape Noun and Verb Stems are mostly monosyllabic: CV, CVC, or disyllabic: CVCV(C); longer words also occur, especially in AFITTI. Many words in AFITTI have a final vowel, absent in NYIMANG, which has no apparent significance

new_statements.relation_note: Type-level agreement only, and only from snippets: Tucker & Bryan (after Stevenson) describe the Nyimang group as tonal with lexically distinctive stress, which matches the catalog's classification of Afitti as a tone language with stress (de Voogt 2009). Differences of detail, not placement: T&B give three tone levels (Stevenson's Nyimang analysis) where de Voogt finds two phonemic tones in Afitti; T&B's stress examples are Nyimang words, so for Afitti proper the visible text is silent on stress. No stress-placement rule is stated by either source, so nothing contradicts the catalog.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Nyimang group (Nyimang and Afitti, data from Stevenson) the chapter reports about three tone levels with lexical and grammatical tone, and adds that stress 'also appears to distinguish words', illustrated with stress-marked Nyimang minimal pairs (body vs adulteress, large turtle vs poor); no rule of stress placement is given and stress is otherwise left unmarked. Nothing Afitti-specific about stress is visible in the accessible fragments: Afitti is mentioned in this stretch only for longer words and a meaningless final vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: none visible; the authors themselves flag that stress is not marked outside the two example pairs
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's chapter treats the 'Nyimang group' = Nyimang (Ama) and Afitti (Dinik), with data from R. C. Stevenson; 'All examples are from NYIMANG, unless otherwise stated', so its tone/stress statements are exemplified on Nyimang, with Afitti cited only for comparative word-shape remarks in the visible fragments. The catalog record rests on de Voogt 2009, fieldwork on Afitti proper (Jebel ed-Dair).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and the domain quotation are verbatim in the extracted text we hold of de Voogt 2009 at Section 8, pp.46-47 (plus the p.44 lengthening remark), exactly as the locator says. (2) Deciding source: a 2009 peer-reviewed phonology sketch (SAL, open access, held as PDF+txt) by the sole modern fieldworker on the language; Glottolog lists no grammar, no other phonology, and Crossref/archive.org/NMLS TOCs/Wikipedia refs surface nothing newer on Afitti prosody. It is the best available description. (3) The classification 'tonal; stress present but no positional rule (free placement in words under five syllables, lexically fixed in longer words)' is a faithful reading of pp.46-48, including the author's own caveat that tone and stress are insufficiently studied. Nothing unheld is likely to change it; the three works still to obtain are older primary/print-only and low priority. (4)
